- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

- **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
  inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
  frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.

## Finishing

- `save --gallery` (or `save --light az,el`) saves the picture lit on its
  relief, as it would be seen on a wall; plain `save` is color only.

- An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
  A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
    Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
    the times at this easel.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

- **Driers.** Oil cooked with litharge, or the siccatives of Courtrai or
  Haarlem, dries much faster but darker and more brittle with too much. Courtrai was "heavily loaded with compounds of lead"; Haarlem was
  copal in oil of spike. Lead white with litharge shrank more and
  aged stiffer than lead white alone (0.9% against 0.5%).
- **Fillers.** Period tube paints held "easily detectable quantities of
  extenders such as kaolin, chalk, talc and barytes"; chalk made
  up 20–47% of some paints analyzed.
- **Bloom.** Dark paint can "become milky or bloomed," linked to glossy dark
  brown tube paints.

period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

I've noted the research files available - every_materials.md and oil_paint_physics.md. Since there's no canvas yet, I need to set one up, but first I should settle on a subject, composition, and format for the painting, working purely from my own knowledge and studio notes rather than external references.

I'm brainstorming possible subjects given the physical paint simulator's strengths - piles, brushes, knives, ground, light - which lend themselves well to landscapes, skies, water, and simple forms. I'm weighing options like a dusk landscape with silhouetted trees and water reflection, a still life with jug and fruit, a bold abstract color field, a harbor scene, a poppy field, or snowy birch trees, trying to pick something achievable yet rich enough to really explore the material.

I'm settling on a landscape idea: a strong sky gradient, distant range at the horizon, a middle ground of field or water, and foreground texture like grasses or stones - something like a stormy coast, a poppy field, or a Mediterranean hill town at evening. I'm also sketching out composition ideas, like an asymmetric layout with a low sun on one side, a tree silhouette on the other, and a river leading the eye into the distance, or an evening salt marsh with banded clouds, reflective wet ground, scattered posts, and a dark mass of reeds - leaning on the simulator's water and sky gradient capabilities.

Now I'm thinking through the practical setup: testing brushes on a scratch canvas first, choosing an aspect ratio like 4/3 or 3/2 for the landscape, and working out how the physical size in mm relates to thread count and pixel pitch so my brush widths translate sensibly into real units. I'm also considering the toned ground option, since the first stroke sets the middle value for the piece.

I'm weighing ground choices — a warm ochre/umber imprimatura versus a cool white lead ground — thinking about how a mid-toned warm wash could unify a sunset landscape and let thin paint glow, versus an absorbent chalk-glue ground that keeps things matte and lean. The ground is essentially the canvas's character, chosen before painting starts, so I'm deciding between oil-glossy and absorbent options.

Now I'm sketching possible subjects with strong value structure that suit the squint-test approach: a sunset over water with a dark shoreline silhouette, a lone tree on a dusk hill, poplars along a river, a harbor with masts, or haystacks with simple rounded light-and-shadow forms. I'm reminding myself the mandate is to paint actual shapes and marks rather than encode an image through masks or computed trickery.

I'm also noting that shapes must each be drawn with their own coordinates rather than mirrored or rotated from another shape's data, and that any built-in form scaffolds should still feel hand-gestured rather than algorithmic. One idea taking shape: a low-tide dusk beach scene, with wet sand reflecting a pale glowing sky, a dark headland silhouette, scattered posts, and a horizon gradient moving from pale lemon upward.

I'm weighing other concept options too — a poppy field under cumulus clouds, a harvest moon over wheat, a lemon still life, or a stormy marsh — but I keep leaning back toward the coastal dusk idea: warm glow at the horizon, cool blue-violet sky and sea above, banded orange-red clouds, and dark silhouetted forms for contrast.

I'm sketching the composition: a dark headland mass at left, maybe a small boat at right, with wet sand reflecting broken color in the foreground leading the eye diagonally toward the glow. I'm also considering the simpler alternative of a single dark tree silhouetted against a dominant sunset gradient as a bolder, more iconic choice.

Thinking through how to render the sky as a graded set of broad horizontal strokes using the simulator's pile-weighting options, and starting to settle on canvas dimensions for the piece.

I need to decide on the ground tone — a warm ochre imprimatura would let sunset warmth glow through thin paint, versus a cooler lead-white base. Since the scratch canvas mirrors the painting's own setup, I'll call canvas{} on the main painting first so the scratch canvas inherits the same ground, then run trials there for the sky gradient mixtures, the wet sand reflections, and the glow before committing to the real painting.

Now I'm settling on canvas parameters: roughly 600×450mm size, a fine-but-visible linen weave around 24×22 threads/cm so texture peeks through thin passes without overwhelming the lay-in, a fixed seed, and a toned ground mixing lead white, yellow ochre, and a touch of raw umber applied thin and fairly even.

I'm weighing knife versus roller application for the ground -- a knife gives a smooth, leveled surface good for the paint to glide over, so I'll go with a light texture setting around 0.15. For the color, I'm testing ratios of lead white to ochre to umber to land on a warm mid-grey value, since a toned ground rather than stark white suits a sunset's bright sky against deep darks.

Now I'm sketching out the composition: a 1000x750 canvas with the horizon around 57-60% down, a low sun partially veiled behind cloud near the right-of-center, and a sky gradient moving from pale lemon near the horizon through orange-rose at the sun to cooler violet-blue up top, with dusky rose-violet cloud bands catching bright orange edges. Below the horizon I'm planning a band of wet sand or sea reflecting the sky's glow in pale streaks against darker gaps, transitioning into foreground wet sand further down.

For the composition I'm placing a dark headland silhouette rising from the left (around x 0-260, peaking near y 330), with maybe a fainter blue-grey headland stacked behind it, and on the right a small boat or mast silhouette dark against the sun's glow as an accent. In the foreground I'm adding a diagonal path of light reflecting toward the sun, with dark pools, ripples, and maybe driftwood, while mapping out the overall value structure—dark masses on the left, bright glow near the horizon, mid-tone sky and sand elsewhere.

I'm now reconsidering whether a straightforward sunset is too conventional, and leaning toward pushing the color bolder—cadmium orange sun, magenta and rose madder clouds, ultramarine/cerulean sky, viridian-Prussian sea, bone-black headland—to make it vivid but still harmonious. I'm also weighing a more distinctive subject than a generic sunset, like upturned fishing boats on a beach at dusk or a lone figure walking the sand, since that would add human presence and a stronger foreground rhythm.

I settle on a coastal dusk scene with two upturned boats at different scales in the foreground for depth, each rendered as a simple hull shape with a warm highlight along the keel. I map out a painting plan across several campaigns: setting up the canvas and testing color mixes on scratch, laying in the big masses (sky, sea, sand, headland, boats), refining sky and cloud details with soft sun glow, adding water reflections and sandy textures, then finishing with boat details and highlights before a final evaluation pass.

I think through practical scale considerations—canvas size in mm, brush widths, and how wet-into-wet blending will work for the sky gradient versus needing drying time between layers—and settle on a canvas setup with a warm buff-toned ground (lead white, yellow ochre, raw umber) applied by knife, reasoning that this warm underlayer will glow nicely through thin cool blue sky strokes and complement the mauve clouds and dark silhouettes. I also plan out specific color mixes for each element: cool blues and violets for the sky, warm oranges and ochres near the sun, dark cool blacks with warm hints for the headland, viridian and Prussian blue for the sea with reflected warm patches, and burnt sienna/Mars red mixes for the boat hulls.

I remind myself to keep shapes and gradients as things I'm deliberately drawing and grading by hand rather than encoding an image through computed masks or proportions—gradients and hand-chosen polygon points are fine, but nothing that amounts to tracing a picture. With the plan set, I finalize the canvas setup call with its size, aspect ratio, linen texture, seed, and ground mixture, and prepare to run it before testing palette piles on scratch.

The studio has no canvas yet, and the palette is empty. I'll start by creating the canvas with a warm, mid-light toned ground so the thin sky colours sit on something warm.

- Drying (scratch, turps-thinned lay-in, lead-white heavy): open for ~5 h, setting ~15 h, tacky ~15-17 h (laid at 09:40, tacky by 06:25 next day).

events.text: size 800

This is a real change. Seen whole, the picture reads as a sunset over a calm sea: a clear sun on the horizon, a glitter path down the water, a dark headland on the left, a sailboat on the right and a pink-violet sky with gold at the horizon. I'll write this assessment in the journal before continuing.

events.name: note
events.text:
Day 34, 06:13 whole-picture review (dry-ish). Reads as a calm sunset over water: sky pink-violet with a blue top and gold at the horizon; sun a clear disc on the horizon with a warm bloom; headland left a dark dome; sailboat right on the glow; glitter path down the sea, tapered glints; sea lilac at horizon to violet and blue at the bottom edge.
Still weak: (1) the headland is a smooth dome with a flat face and the pale peach-cream patch beside its right slope reads as a soft cloud/haze: fine, but its edge is blobby; (2) the sea's lower corners and mid-sea streaks are a bit busy with stripes; (3) the top sky has many horizontal stripes (broad strokes) and a blue-violet band; (4) the stray pink blob at top right (800,64) is still open; (5) the path foot is rounded and a bit pale against the violet sea (acceptable).
Keep: sun, path, boat, horizon, palette harmony. Next: quiet the top sky stripes with a dry-ish wash only if it sets cleanly, cover the pink blob with body, and check the headland edge once more before finishing.

I'm examining the upper-left sky region closely, noting the grey-lavender texture, mapping a green streak's pixel coordinates to canvas position, and spotting scattered yellow flecks of bare ground.

These blotchy cells look like soap bubbles from the broad dabbing strokes. The greenish tint is likely a mixing artifact from blue overlapping warm ground tones, which I could cover with a violet-blue touch.

Stepping back, I'm assessing the whole painting honestly: the sea and sun/horizon feel solid, the headland dome is a bit stiff but acceptable, the top sky stripes look slightly mechanical but passable, and there's a stray pink blob in the upper-right sky I should address.

Checking that pink blob's position in the full view, it actually reads fine as a small cloud, so I'll leave it. The sea's lilac-to-violet-to-blue gradation works, and a pale lilac streak near the left edge looks okay too. To elevate the piece further, I'm considering adding distant features like a far island ridge or a second smaller headland on the right horizon.

I'm weighing whether more depth-giving ripples or cloud shadows on the sea are worth adding, though the composition already feels balanced with its bold violet sunset palette. Given the considerable time already spent, I think it's best to wrap up with a few targeted fixes: covering the green tint at top right, refining the headland silhouette, checking the pale patch beside it, and adding a signature — so I'll zoom into the headland and sea edges at full detail to judge these final touches.
The upper-left sky is a soft gradient, with a faint green cast top right and scattered bare-ground flecks. Those are minor. Next I'll check the headland and the cloud patch beside it at full detail.

Looking closely, the headland's dark mottled mass has its right slope edge blurring into the cloud patch nearby, with that cream/white smear showing streaky horizontal texture. The coral bank reads fine, and the pale cloud patch above the slope looks acceptable with its streaky brushwork, though I'm still checking the headland's silhouette edge.

Overall the piece feels pleasant and in decent shape, but I want to consider a few finishing touches: slightly darkening the headland's lower portion to ground it against the warm glow, and perhaps tinting that cream cloud patch with more rose to better align with the coral bank below. The sky's stripe texture seems fine as part of the broad-brush look, and the sun's bright disc with warm bloom looks good. I'm now thinking about addressing the green cast in the top-right corner as a final touch.

Checking that pink blob near the top edge, it reads fine as a small cloud accent. For a title I'm leaning toward "Low Sun on Calm Water" rather than some of the other options I considered. Before calling it done, I want to look at the whole painting once more in gallery mode and do a final value squint check, asking myself honestly whether I'm happy with it or want to push it further.

At full detail the headland's right slope is softened by the earlier blend, and the cream patch beside it reads as a haze, which I can live with. Next I'll look at the picture in the gallery light, the way it will hang, and check the value structure once more.

events.name: look
events.text: mode gallery, size 800

Checking the gallery view, things read well: the warm golden horizon band behind the boat looks right, the sun's position lines up correctly on canvas, the lilac sun path with glints works, the dark headland dome holds, and the blue band at the top reads correctly too.

The faint lilac streak at the left edge and the violet-blue lower sea both work fine, and the mid-lilac banded water in the middle reads naturally. Overall this feels like a solid sunset composition, though I'm weighing whether to push further -- maybe a touch more glow around the sun, or a faint distant island silhouette on the right horizon to balance the composition and add depth.

A warm rim light on the headland's top ridge might help but earlier attempts at that came out dry or failed with a glaze, so I'll skip it. I'm fairly satisfied with the piece now, but want to double check a couple small spots -- the pink cloud shape near the top right looks fine, but there may be an unwanted faint green or teal tint near the top band that I should examine closely and cover with violet if it's noticeable.

The gallery light holds the picture: the sun, the glitter path, the sailboat and the headland read together. The one thing I want to check before I finish is a faint green cast in the top sky, left of centre.

I'm pinpointing the greenish streaks in the upper sky, roughly around canvas x 330-425, y 30-46, and tracing them to where the lilac-blue mixes with yellow pigment in that region.

This confirms a known effect: thin cerulean laid over a warm buff ground reads as green-grey, which explains the cast. To fix it, I'd need a body-thick coat of ultramarine-violet over the now-dry sky, applied in broad strokes since blending into dry paint won't work the same as wet-on-wet.

Given the risk versus the minor visual impact, though, I'm leaning toward accepting the green cast as a subtle, almost natural teal-at-zenith effect rather than risking an uneven patch—it's really only noticeable in close crop, not in the full gallery view. Shifting focus to the rest of the composition, the sea's lower half and glitter path both look solid, though the path's base has a slightly hard-edged lilac wedge worth softening.

Reviewing the full painting now—the sun, headland, sailboat, and sky bands all read well, with only minor touches like the lilac haze at the horizon base being negligible. For final enhancements, I'm weighing whether to add subtle horizontal cloud streaks near the horizon for atmosphere, though the existing pink bands already feel complete, and considering whether a faint reflection of the boat in the water below would add a nice finishing touch.

A few low-risk dashes under the hull in the boat's dark color at lower opacity would strengthen the water's presence, though it might come across as fussy, and warming the headland's sun-facing slope didn't work when I tried it earlier. I think the painting is essentially done, but I want to double-check whether the slight green cast at the top of the sky is noticeable enough to need fixing—looking at it again, it reads more as cool air at the zenith, which feels acceptable rather than a flaw. A wet glaze to unify the sky won't work since glazes pool on dry paint, so I'll leave that area as is and move on to checking the pink blob near the top right.

The green cast is a small patch of thin cerulean laid over the warm buff ground, so it reads as cool air rather than a mistake. I'll note it and check the lower sea, where I laid the test ripples, for leftover marks.

I'm examining the lower sea area, which reads as a dark violet with soft lumps and a blurred, mostly dark band, with faint light dashes near the bottom right. It passes as calm deep water in dusk light, though the earlier teal pebble trial I tested on scratch doesn't seem to show up here in any noticeable way.

Thinking ahead, I want to add a small reflection of the schooner in the water, maybe a few more gleam marks near the path to tie things together, and consider a title and signature before handoff. I should also check the top-right area where I painted over a pink blob, to make sure it's cleaned up now.
The lower sea is a soft, dark violet with a few light ripples at its foot, which reads as deep calm water. Next I'll check the top-right blob, which I covered with body paint.

That pink-lilac patch still reads as a small cloud in the blue sky, though its hard edge gives it a slightly stain-like quality. It's small and high enough in the scene that I think it works fine as is, so I'll leave it alone.
The blob now reads as a small pink cloud. Its edge is a little hard, so I'll see how far it has set before deciding whether to shape it as a cloud.

events.name: note
events.text:
Cloud episode, top sky, day 36-40 (lesson, not a recipe to repeat): (1) a body cloud (ultramarine .4 + alizarin .5 + white .7 underside, pale cadmium .5 + rose .2 + white 1.4 top) over a blue sky, one sitting: the magenta underside is saturated and reads as a purple stain; the cream top reads as a separate lemon puff. (2) A dry flat-7 lilac scumble (cerulean .6 + alizarin .2 + white 1.0, load .14, pressure .08-.13) across it broke the magenta into grey-lilac flecks, reading as weave, not as haze. (3) A rose-pink cover over the cloud (cerulean .7 + alizarin .35 + rose .2 + white 1.4, body, load 1.0): covered too big, rose-pink, too pink for the sky. (4) A sky-blue cover (cerulean .9 + alizarin .2 + white 1.3, broad, edge lost) laid over the open pink mixed it into a streaked smear with the mask edge showing.
Conditions: all laid on sky dry-to-tacky at 14:00 day 36-40 with the top sky dry. Hypothesis: a small cloud over a blue sky needs a value and temperature close to its surround; keep the cloud pale and cool, and keep magenta out of cool skies; stop covering a passage more than twice.

events.text:
Looking at the full composition now as a fresh viewer: a calm sunset over a violet sea, with a blue sky fading into rose and gold bands, the sun glowing at the horizon with a glitter path streaming down the center, a dark headland on the left, a sailboat to the right, and something pale forming in the upper right corner.

The pale upper-right block reads as a lilac cloud bank, though its left edge is too sharp and slab-like to feel natural, while the sea below shifts nicely from pale lilac near the horizon to deep violet in the foreground, with the glitter path and gold horizon glow working well overall.

Below the horizon, there's a lighter oval patch in the sea that reads as a subtle grey-lilac sheen, which seems fine as is. The lower-left corner is just plain violet, nothing notable there.

The real weak point remains that top-right block — a pale, cool-lilac mass with a hard edge that feels disconnected from the rose tones in the sky, like it was pasted in rather than painted as part of the same light.

Past fixes have failed because rectangular covers and dry-brushed veils don't blend into organic sky shapes, and glazes over tacky paint just lift and spread the color underneath. The edge needs softening through value and temperature matching on fully dry paint, not through a flat patch, so I'm thinking the fix is to paint a new cloud shape that overlaps that left edge with rose/violet tones matching the surrounding sky, letting the block's edge dissolve into the interior of a believable cloud mass rather than sitting as a seam.

Stepping back, the painting feels like a coherent, successful sunset with a few honest imperfections I could choose to accept. If I'm asking what I'd genuinely enjoy improving further, it's the sea in the foreground -- right now it's a flat, uniform violet with horizontal banding, and it could come alive with reflected rose and gold light near the horizon and a subtler reflection under the sailboat.

But I keep circling back to the lesson from the handoff notes: every fix attempted so far has introduced new problems, so the safer path is fewer, smaller, carefully tested changes rather than another sweeping repair. Checking the value structure, that top-right block reads at a similar lightness to the sun-glow patch and the pale cloudy area near the headland, so it's genuinely competing with the sun and light-path for visual attention even though those are meant to be the focal points.

Looking closer at the block's layered history, it's already got a rose cloud body plus an earlier feathered cover, with the upper portion blue, middle cerulean-rose, and the base fading into rose-lilac where it meets the pink sky band — so piling on another gradient cover risks just adding a third layer of fuss rather than resolving the real issue, which is where its edges meet the sky in value and hue.

I think I'll accept the block as a pale distant haze serving as a compositional counterweight to the headland, as the earlier handoff decided, and instead audit other areas: the sea horizon line, the mid-sea bands, the lower sea reflections, the headland/ledge, and the sun's glow, weighing whether any deserve risk given how often prior interventions went wrong. The horizon, sea bands, and headland all look acceptable on inspection, so the main candidates left are the sun's glow and sea-reflection near it, plus the overall balance between the central path and the sailboat — but none feel urgent enough to justify disruptive changes.

Given the many past failures, I'm leaning toward a cautious approach: a few small, tested improvements rather than sweeping changes, so I want to pull detail crops of the sea left/right near the horizon, the headland/ledge, and the bottom band to check them at 1:1 before deciding where effort is actually warranted.

The whole picture in colour reads as a calm sunset: blue top, rose and gold bands, a pale sun with its glitter path, the dark headland left and the sailboat right. The top-right block is the most conspicuous passage. Next I'll check the sun, boat and right-hand sea at 1:1, then the headland and the sea's lower corners.

Checking the right crop: the sun reads as a pale-yellow disc with warm halo, the sailboat silhouette is clear against a golden sky, and the horizon line is crisp where gold meets lilac sea—overall this section looks good.

Moving to the lower-left crop, I notice the horizon has dark dashes marking distant ridge details, the sea below transitions from a light lilac-pink band into mottled purple-violet blocks with visible brush-stroke edges. The blocky texture isn't ideal for a distant sea but reads as acceptable paint texture.

Now I'm weighing candidate fixes. The top-right pale lilac-cream slab is the most conspicuous issue—its hard vertical left edge stands out, though its lower boundary aligns with the distant ridge peak, so it could pass as a hazy cloud bank over hills if I soften that left edge. Turning to the sea, I'm checking whether the mid and lower bands' color transitions hold together convincingly.

The top-left dark violet band and horizontal pink band look fine. The headland remains a plain dark dome—a smooth silhouette against the sky that's been flagged repeatedly for lacking detail, but past attempts to add a shoulder or crest notch by stacking shapes have failed, so I'm considering instead painting a single new outline polygon that overlaps and reshapes the whole dome rather than adding onto it, keeping in mind the dark body is now fully dry after being laid down days ago.

Checking the sun, glitter path, the pale grey-lilac oval patch in the sea, and the rounded pale foot of the path—all of these read acceptably at this scale, so the piece feels like it's reached an accepted state, which leaves me weighing whether further work is even worthwhile.

As a painter, I'd say the strongest elements are the sun, the glitter path, and the sailboat against the gold horizon, while the weakest is the uniform violet sea with its blocky strokes and the top-right slab. I'd considered adding a subtle warm gold-peach reflection beside the sun path and boat, but that's already present, and the foreground sea is already darkened for depth—so I'm left examining whether the mottled, blocky texture in the mid-sea still needs smoothing out.

Given the risk of repeated repairs and that the piece already reads coherently, I'm weighing whether to make a few careful, low-risk refinements versus leaving things as-is, especially around the top-right block's hard left edge—options range from accepting it outright, to adding an organic cloud overlap, to softening the seam with a broad wash of the block's own color.

I realize the wash approach would create another hard edge on dry paint, and scraping or lifting won't work since the paint has already passed its gel point—so the block is effectively unliftable now. The only remaining route to alter it is another body cover with an organic, feathered edge like the one that successfully hid the saturated rose earlier.

A second organic cover straddling the current hard edge, graded in color to blend both sides, could soften the seam, though a narrow band risks reading as a pillar rather than a blend—this feels like a real but uncertain option. A safer path might just be waiting: the handoff notes it's worth checking whether the top-right block reads better after more drying time, and it's been about 45 days since that cover was applied.

Stepping back, I'm asking whether the picture as a whole feels emotionally satisfying—and overall it does, with the warm-cool sunset glow, glitter path, and nice sky rhythm, though I still have reservations about the top-right slab, the flat violet foreground sea, and the plainness of the headland. If I pushed further, the foreground sea seems like the most worthwhile target: right now it's a flat, even violet with blocky strokes, when a calm sunset sea should show more luminous reflected color—darker blue-violet from the sky above blending with warm pink reflections from the clouds.

Checking where ripple strokes already exist, I see rose and peach touches scattered around y440-540 and y700-750, but the broad middle band from about y550-700 across much of the canvas is just flat violet or purple blocks with no ripple texture at all—that's the gap I should fill to make the water read convincingly rather than as a solid color field.

Adding a sparse set of ripples there with the same accepted flat-3, load-0.3, pressure-.07-.13 technique seems low-risk, though the guide suggests foreground ripples near the viewer should be longer and bolder than the distant ones, so I'd want to scale stroke length up toward 120-150 for that nearer band while watching out for it reading as repetitive stripes.

I should trial this on scratch-26 first, which already has a sea coat re-laid and dried over roughly twelve days, making it a reasonable stand-in for testing ripple strokes on the lower sea before committing on the actual painting. The current foreground reads as one flat violet, which earlier reviews flagged as lacking a darker bottom, so some ripple work there might genuinely help rather than just add visual noise.

Now the sea actually has a dark bottom band that reads convincingly as deep water, with a pale lilac horizon strip and a mottled mid-violet zone that already suggests a water surface fairly well. Adding sparkle or ripple texture seems like a worthwhile, modest refinement since there's an accepted recipe for it in the handoff notes, but I'm wary of prior feedback calling the sea's lower corners and mid-sea streaks "a bit busy with stripes" — so I'm leaning toward fewer, softer ripples confined to specific bands and limited horizontal ranges, using low-opacity lilac or peach tones, maybe echoing the glow near the path foot as a subtle reflection.

The path foot itself already reads fine as a pale, rounded glow fading into a dark purple border, like a soft reflection — I'll leave that alone.

I'm starting to feel the painting is close to a good finishing point, though I know I could keep refining indefinitely. One more consideration is composition balance: the top-right pale cloud mass, the sailboat at mid-height, and the central sun all concentrate more light on the right side, while the left has the dark headland and the sea's bottom is dark too, so I want to think through whether that asymmetry works or needs adjusting.

I'm weighing whether to add a value gradient to soften the top-right cloud's left edge, but any changes to that area are risky since there's no undo and the condition would need replicating carefully before testing on scratch material.

Given the painting's stable state, I decide a full trial reproducing the sky stack is too costly, and instead accept the top-right block as a plausible distant cloud bank despite its somewhat crisp left edge. I turn my attention to the sea instead, since it's the largest and least resolved area, and think about adding subtle horizontal reflections and ripples in the mid-foreground to tie the sky's colors into the water while avoiding past mistakes with busy, striped textures.

I plan to test this ripple idea on scratch-26, which already has a comparable sea coat laid down and dried, checking its drying status and visual similarity to the painting before committing to specific tones, stroke lengths, and placement that avoid the path and its pale, rounded foot. I also reconsider the overall composition — the horizon-centered balance between sky and sea, the sun's position, and the pale lilac patch near the path top — concluding they're acceptable, and decide to view the scratch's current state first before running the trial.

The sun, boat and right-hand sea read well, and the boat silhouette works. The lower sea shows blocky stroke ends, and its mid-foreground (y 540–680) has no horizontal ripple marks, so it reads as a flat violet field. Before I decide on any change, I'll look at the scratch canvas, whose sea coat was laid with the same recipe, as a fair trial surface.

**Evening Light on Still Water**

A calm sunset over a violet sea. A pale sun sits on the horizon with a warm bloom, and a broken glitter path runs down the water toward the viewer. A dark headland anchors the left, and a small sailboat with its reflection sits on the glow at right. The sky moves from blue at the top through lilac and rose cloud bands to gold at the horizon. This sitting, the lower sea got horizontal water glints that grow toward the viewer, so it reads as water rather than a flat field. The top-right cloud bank stays heavy, and the sea has one dark streak. I accept both, and I'm content with the picture as a whole.

*Accepted, with reasons (judged at full detail):*
- Lower-left near glints: bright, rounded white pills at 1:1, but they read as glints at whole-view scale. Any cover would add a new shape. If I return, lay the near band at pressure 0.07–0.10 with cooler, lower-white mixes.

- Headland ledge, rock and waterline: part of the dome's flank. Small dark reflection dashes tie the base to the water, so no foam is needed.
- Path foot, sky stipple flecks and sun: accepted as they are.

*Practical lessons that still apply:*
- A dense body dark (load 1.0) on dry sea took about 10 days to dry: setting at 5, tacky at 8, dry at 10. The earlier 3–5 day estimate is too short for full-load bodies.
- Water glints on a dry dark sea: flat 3, load 0.3, pressure 0.07–0.11, horizontal, 18–74 units long (longer nearer), in lilac, grey-teal, teal and peach mixes, kept off the path column. Pressure above about 0.12 with white-rich mixes gives pills.
- Name a fresh scratch by its log file once it exists. I mislabelled one this sitting and corrected the journal.

*Uncertain:* whether a body cloud on open sky would have held better, and whether the near-band pills would read better dimmer. Both are untested.

- To use what worked, paint it on the painting: the same pile, the same handling.
- `new_scratch: true` (with `scratch: true`) puts the scratch canvas aside and starts a
  fresh one before the chunk runs. The old log stays, as `paintings/lua/scratch-1.lua`, and so on.
- A trial judges a passage only as far as it repeats that passage's conditions: lay the
  underlayer you mean to work over, and let it dry as long as it has on the painting.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
    Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
    the times at this easel.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

- **Shape the mask like the passage.** Mask wipes start and stop a little
  inside the mask, so a rectangle leaves a frame of the wiped color. If a
  frame shows, wipe along its sides with a path.
- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.

## Finishing

- `save --gallery` (or `save --light az,el`) saves the picture lit on its
  relief, as it would be seen on a wall; plain `save` is color only.

- An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
  A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

Given the brief allows accepted imperfections, and this seam has already been let stand twice before, I'm weighing whether re-litigating it is worth the risk versus simply accepting it and following a different thread of interest instead.

Looking back at the overall painting, the real standouts are the sunset, sun, glitter path, and sailboat, while the headland dome, seam, lower-left pills, and sheen oval are all accepted quirks. slopeP = {{140,322},{160,326},{186,338},{214,352},{246,370},{280,388},{312,402},{336,412},{352,421}}
function dSlope(x, y)
  local best = 1e9
  for i = 1, #slopeP - 1 do
    local ax, ay = slopeP[i][1], slopeP[i][2]
    local bx, by = slopeP[i+1][1], slopeP[i+1][2]
    local dx, dy = bx - ax, by - ay
    local t = clamp(((x-ax)*dx + (y-ay)*dy) / (dx*dx + dy*dy), 0, 1)
    local px, py = ax + t*dx, ay + t*dy
    local d = ((x-px)^2 + (y-py)^2)^0.5
    if d < best then best = d end
  end
  return best
end
function litW(x, y)
  local near = 1 - clamp(dSlope(x, y) / 40, 0, 1)
  return clamp(near * clamp((x - 120) / 200, 0, 1), 0, 1)
end

events.text:
Looking at full scale, those dashes read as blue-lilac cloud shadows with soft, slightly ragged edges rather than stuck-on shapes — they pass as acceptable cloud streaks within the rose band.

Turning to the top-right pale block, repeated attempts to cover it have failed, but the last organic feathered cover with heavy blur apparently worked, reading as a cloud contour at whole-view scale even though it still shows a fairly straight vertical edge. Given how well the graded mass change worked on the headland — reshaping the existing mass rather than adding a new cover — I'm considering applying that same approach to re-lay the cloud mass in the top-right block.

The risk is that the block's wrongness lies in its silhouette itself, specifically the straight left wall, so any mask that extends or retracts that edge will likely leave a seam where it meets the much older, drier underlayer, unlike the headland where the underlayer was a close value match.

Looking again at the whole view, the left wall of the block really does read as the strongest straight edge in the picture—a near-vertical boundary from top down to about y=120 separating the blue-violet sky from the pale mauve mass—which is the most criticized element across sittings. Weighing the options: either accept the piece as finished per the handoff's advice, or risk a graded re-lay on the scratch to test whether the edge can be softened without creating a visible seam.

I've got plenty of time to experiment, but the journal's record of past damage from over-covering argues for discipline—testing any change on a matching scratch patch first, with the same underlayer and age, rather than directly on the painting. The trouble is that replicating the actual top-right block's layered history (a rose body dried under a blue cap, built up over a prior cloud base) on a fresh scratch patch is a complex reconstruction, and the journal explicitly warns that trials on a mismatched underlayer aren't a fair test. A more modest alternative would just be checking whether the straightness of that left wall is actually a problem at whole-view distance before committing to any intervention at all.

Looking at the whole view again, the sea's mid-left band now reads fine, so my real remaining concerns are the top-right block's straight left wall, the upper-left streak, and the lower-left pills. The handoff notes say to re-judge after a season had passed and then accept, which the previous sitting did at 1:1 scale seeing an organic curve—but at whole view that same edge now reads as a noticeably straight ~120px line, which feels like enough to warrant a careful, organic, graded re-lay of just that left wall rather than leaving it as is.

The horizon base and warm reflection under the sun look lovely at whole view. I'm considering testing an organic wall-softening on the scratch using a stand-in underlayer that mimics the block's dry time, then applying the same feathered cover recipe that worked before but with a bending S-curve mask and a wider blur — though honestly the marginal benefit feels small against the risk of introducing a new artifact.

The journal's biggest lesson is that each added cover compounds damage, and I've already made a meaningful improvement with the headland light and two glint additions. I'm tempted to pursue my curiosity about the top-right wall's straightness with one careful, low-risk test — but I realize any change to that edge requires painting on one side or the other, and painting the sky side counts as a cover while painting the block side just adjusts its value.

So the safer approach mirrors the headland method: regrade the block's own interior near the edge, darkening and blueing its left zone so it blends toward the sky's value, without extending the mask beyond the block's existing silhouette. That way the wall softens in value rather than shifting in position, keeping it a value gradient within the mass rather than a new cover.

But I realize this is riskier than the headland case since the headland's new paint sat close in value to its dark underlayer, while the block is pale — so a darker cover there risks creating a visible band or pillar rather than a smooth fade. A fair scratch trial isn't really possible since the block's underlayer stack is too complex to replicate honestly, so testing this on scratch would be misleading. Given that, the honest choice is to leave the block as is and record the reasoning in the journal, treating it as the accepted heavy cloud accent.

I also go through a final checklist: confirming the sea glints stay within their masks and don't cross the horizon or overlap the sun path or sailboat reflection, verifying the headland's ledge and rock stay contained within the graded mass, and deciding not to push the lit slope further since the mass has already been re-layered multiple times. I decide against signing the painting, treating the title as sufficient identity, and move toward journaling judgements on each open passage — the streak, block, pills, sheen oval, headland, path, sun, and cream patch — before doing one more 1:1 check on the left-middle sea glints to resolve my lingering concern about them reading as pebbles rather than ripples.

At 1:1 the dashes are soft-edged blue-violet cloud streaks in the rose band, not stuck-on shapes, so I accept them. Next I'll check the left-middle glints I added this sitting at 1:1, since at the whole-view scale a few read as pale pebbles.

I'm examining this cropped region closely, noting several faint glint marks—a pale cyan-white bar, a teal cluster, and small peach and pale dots scattered at specific pixel coordinates—trying to map their exact positions on the canvas.

These glints look sparse and broken, which reads as acceptable shimmer at whole-view scale, especially against the lilac horizon wash above. I've already rechecked the upper sea area to the right and accepted it, so now I want to revisit the top-right block one more time to be honest about my judgment, particularly looking at how the rose-mauve mass's near-vertical left edge reads as a cloud bank at whole view.

The curved lower-left edge and blue cap at top give it an organic quality that I accept, since repair attempts (rectangular patch, feathered edge, band) all failed given the layered, mixed-age underlayer — any new cover would just add another conflicting object. The accent also balances nicely against the headland on the left side. Now I'm ready to write up the journal entry covering the graded headland method, the glint trials, the dim lower-left pills decision, and the upper-left streak hypothesis.

Testing the blend-over-lean-paint theory confirms it reproduces the grainy weave texture, while a sky-matched cover attempt just creates an unwanted pale oval, so I'm accepting the streak as a weave artifact invisible at whole-view scale. I'm working through the remaining accept/reject calls: the top-right block, the stray blue streaks in the rose band, and the sheen oval, all of which read fine as natural variations at whole-view distance even though they're more pronounced at 1:1 — so I'm accepting each with their stated reasoning.

Finishing up, I'm logging a few practical lessons for the handoff journal: graded re-lays over dry dark masses can reshape form without adding new shapes, and blends over lean paint reliably leave a grainy weave with pale islands, while covering that grain with body paint just dries into a rejected pale oval.

Separately, the dim cool glints read as fine dotted texture at close view but as glints from afar, and the mid-sea horizontal glints give the mid sea useful structure — both accepted. I'm now trying to untangle which scratch file numbering corresponds to which trial (headland, thin-patch, blend test, cover trial) since the tool's auto-logged names got confusing across this sitting, and I need to sort out which scratch-28/29/30 maps to which experiment before finalizing the notes.

I've worked out the mapping now: scratch-29.lua holds the headland and sea trials, scratch-30.lua holds the thin-patch sky work, and the current scratch.lua holds both the blend test and the streak cover trial. Now I need to go back through my previously flagged unresolved items — the lower-left glints, the sheen oval, the headland ledge, the path foot, and the slate sky stipple flecks — and actually look at each one closely enough to render a real judgement rather than relying on memory, so I'll pull fresh detail crops of the sheen oval, path foot, and sky flecks before writing anything down.

At 1:1 the left-middle glints are sparse, short and broken, and a few small pale pieces read as glints, not pebbles. I accept them. Before writing my judgements, I'll inspect the remaining passages the handoff listed: the sheen oval, the path foot, and the slate stipple flecks.

Three findings at 1:1:
- The sheen oval (around 566,480) reads as a dark violet streak in the sea, consistent with the handoff's acceptance.
- The path foot is pale and dissolves into the gold dashes above it, and the glitter there is bright, sharp, elongated flecks, which read as glitter.
- The top-right block's left wall is a curved, organic cloud edge, and the slate stipple flecks read as weave catching light, as the handoff recorded.

Each of these was judged before, and each still holds at 1:1. I'll now record my reflections in the journal and decide where to stop.

I'm checking whether I'm genuinely satisfied with the sunset-over-water piece before wrapping up, since the brief asks me to only finish once I'm happy and have recorded reflections and a handoff. I just reworked the headland, so I want to verify that change actually reads well before calling it done.

I checked the dark band at 1:1 and it still reads as the silhouette edge against the lit slope, which works fine at whole-view scale. The glints and sheen placements don't overlap the sun path, so that's settled. What's worth noting is that the graded mass re-lay actually succeeded this sitting — it's a genuinely new technique rather than another cover, and I'm wondering if the same value-gradient approach could help the top-right cloud block.

The journal describes that cloud as a flat, accepted pale mauve mass, and I'd noted earlier that clouds read as form through a gradient of value and temperature across the whole shape. The headland success came from laying a gradient directly over a dark existing mass with a much lighter warm mix, which is different from the earlier flat covers that failed because they sat as a different value over the surround — so the key distinction is gradient-over-mass versus flat-color-over-edge.

Now I'm weighing whether to try the same graded re-lay on the top-right cloud, the largest pale mass in the upper sky, which has a blue cap, pink body, and organic left wall and has stayed unchanged and accepted for 90 days. The risk is that this is the biggest, most complex passage in the sky, and past attempts there produced stiff rectangular slabs until an organic polygon mask with roughening and blur finally worked — so a graded cover might only succeed if the mask stays organic like that. I'm also considering whether this is worth pursuing at all, since the headland was the change I actually enjoyed, the sea is now resolved as water, and the cloud is the one remaining open question.

I'm deciding the top-right block reads fine as a cloud at whole view despite being slightly heavy and slate-colored at the top, and the journal already accepted it after a season, so I'll leave it alone rather than risk a graded re-lay there. Going through my list of previously flagged passages, everything's now been judged and accepted or improved except one I haven't rechecked this sitting — a violet block on the far-right edge near the boat that was flagged as an open issue days ago and was supposed to be addressed by an earlier repair but was dropped from later summary lists, so I want to inspect it at full resolution along with the boat/schooner area before calling this done. I'll pull a close crop of the right side near the boat to check for any leftover hard edges, then move toward writing the final journal handoff and closing reply once I've confirmed everything reads well.

The journal is up to date. Before finishing, I want to check two passages I haven't inspected at 1:1 this sitting: the right-hand sky by the sailboat, where the earlier notes recorded a violet block at the far-right edge, and the boat itself.

The right side is working well now — the rose cloud band, gold horizon, and sailboat silhouette with its mainsail, jib, and hull all read cleanly, and the stray violet block is gone. But I'm noticing some odd vertical striping or dotted texture near the top-left of this crop that needs a closer look.

That texture turns out to be just the weave catching the light, not an actual defect, so everything passes. I'm tempted to go back and rework the top-right cloud since it's the largest, heaviest pale mass, but I remember my own rule against revisiting a passage more than twice — and this one's already been covered many times — so I'll leave it as is and consider the piece finished, moving on to write the final handoff note titled "Evening Light on Still Water."

I'm jotting down the practical lessons to carry forward: that a graded re-lay of dry paint with an organic clip mask reads as a lit form by shifting value across the mass rather than adding a stroke on top; that glints at low pressure read convincingly as water when repeated across zones; that blending over lean paint leaves visible weave and color artifacts so it should be avoided; and a few other observations about covering pale ovals and cool bands on the sea.

I'm also confirming the dry time of a full-load dark body on a dry base is about 12 days, matching my earlier estimate, and noting a small labeling mistake I made with a scratch file name. I'm flagging remaining uncertainties — whether the graded method would fix the troubled top-right cloud, and whether the bright pills should read dimmer on the actual painting rather than just on scratch.

Now I'm thinking about how to close out: the brief wants a title and a few sentences about the picture, plus a concise handoff recording lessons and open questions for next time. I'll skip signing, since earlier sittings didn't, and move to drafting that final note.

Both passages check out. The rose cloud band reads as soft streaks, and the far-right violet block is gone. The sailboat is a clean silhouette with hull, mainsail, jib and mast. Nothing else needs a repair, and the top-right block has already had more covers than my notes allow. I'll record the final judgements and handoff.

**Evening Light on Still Water**

A calm sunset over a violet sea. A pale sun sits on the horizon with a warm bloom, and a broken glitter path runs down the water toward the viewer. Stepping back, the handoff recommends accepting the upper-left streak, and I've tested a repair that confirms that decision. Still, after three sittings, I want to check freshly against my own sense of the piece, asking whether there's anything I'd actually enjoy pushing further rather than just following the recommendation. I'm looking again at the whole-view normal-colour image to see what genuinely stands out to me.

The composition is a sunset with violet sea, pale sun, glitter path, a dark lit headland on the left, a sailboat against the horizon glow on the right, and a sky graded from blue to rose/lilac to gold, with a heavy mauve slab in the top-right reading as a cloud bank. That slab catches my attention — the graded re-lay technique worked well on the headland, turning a dry mass into something that reads as lit, but I never tested that same approach on this cloud, and I'd flagged it explicitly as an open question despite my rule against covering a passage more than twice.

I'm weighing whether to risk another pass on that block, given prior cloud-cover attempts there already caused damage, but the graded re-lay is methodically distinct from a flat cover and deserves a scratch test — same underlayer, a clipped graded re-lay following the cloud's outline with cool blue at top fading to warm lilac/rose below, moderate coverage and load, then judged at full view. The complication is that the block isn't a clean shape but a feathered rose form with a curved edge, so I'd need the same soft mask with blur to constrain the graded piles properly.

Checking the other notes: the sun path's pale pool reads fine in the full view but shows straight trapezoid edges at 1:1 that break the illusion of glitter, since the mask boundary sits right against the untouched sea coat. The lower-left pills and headland pass inspection as-is.

Overall the picture feels largely finished, and I'm weighing whether to keep refining versus stopping now that I'm content with it. The strongest lingering concern is the top-right pale mauve mass — it balances the headland well in the whole view, but its left edge remains a hard value step the journal already flagged as the weakest passage in the piece.

I'm thinking about whether a graded re-lay trick, like the one that made the headland read as convincingly lit, could soften that cloud's hard edge. Since the sunset light hits it from below, its underside should glow warm while the top stays cooler — which is roughly already true, but it still reads as stacked layers rather than a unified lit form. It feels worth doing a quick scratch trial to test if a graded re-lay smooths that transition, since it's the one open question the previous handoff left unresolved.

Though the self-imposed rule against adding more covers to an already-worked block makes me hesitant — a graded re-lay is a different technique than a flat cover, since it changes the mass's value rather than adding a shape, but it's still risky on a block with this much history. If I clip the graded colour to the same mask, I'll just reproduce the same hard edge, so the mask itself would need to be widened on the left for the gradient to actually feather into the sky.

But widening the mask means overlapping into the sky, which creates a visible seam where the new pass meets the old sky colour — the classic failure mode. Looking at the whole composition honestly, the block already reads convincingly as a cloud bank balancing the dark headland, with the sun and boat anchoring the right side, so I don't think chasing the cloud further is worth the risk; if anything, I'd rather turn my attention to the sea and the glitter path, though that's already been resolved in earlier sittings.

Examining the path's boundaries more closely — the trapezoidal glint area sits against the sea coat with a soft diagonal edge — it reads fine as a glitter path at full view, not as a hard road edge. Given the pattern of past damage from adding covers, the disciplined conclusion is that the painting is in a good, finished state and further intervention carries more risk than reward, even though part of me wants to keep pushing.

If I were to pursue one more thing for enjoyment, it'd be the top-right cloud's graded re-lay, since that's the handoff's open question and the largest pale mass — worth testing on a scratch replicate first (sky lay, then cloud block, dried, then graded re-lay) and only applying to the real painting if it's a clear improvement, while acknowledging a scratch test can't fully replicate the original's layered history.

That said, I'm not sure the top-right block is actually a problem worth this effort — at whole view it reads clearly as a cloud bank balancing the headland, and while it's maybe the least satisfying passage, it isn't glaring, so I should still give it an honest, explicit judgment per the handoff's instructions.

I've now gone through each unresolved passage: rejected the streak repair with reason (the failure turned out to be textural, not about hue, which is a useful finding), and accepted the top-right block, lower-left pills, sheen oval, headland ridge, and path foot, each with reasoning. I'm now considering whether there's anything else worth pursuing, starting to look again at how the sea reads.

The sea reads fine with its violet base and horizontal glints, the sun works as a focal point with its pale warm bloom, and the glitter path functions well as the leading line — overall the painting feels resolved enough, with remaining weaknesses accepted for good reasons. Since further covers have only added damage, the one idea still worth testing is a graded re-lay of the cloud block; I could trial this on scratch first since it's low-risk if only applied after a clean test, and it addresses the composition's most noticeable value step — the journal itself suggests either accepting it as a softened pale veil or removing it with a broad cover once the whole passage is settled.

My prior sittings were explicit though: don't repaint the top-right block again, it's already had more than two covers, and each new layer risks making it thicker and more slab-like. A graded re-lay would still be a new cover, and the counter-argument is strong — six-plus layers have hardened it, and a fresh scratch trial can't truly replicate 250 days of multi-layered aging anyway, since the journal's own experience showed scratch replicates of this exact passage have been misleading before (the scratch cover that looked fine turned into a rose slab on the painting). Given that history, I think the honest choice is to respect my earlier decisions and leave the cloud block alone, noting the untested question in the handoff for a future sitting with a more faithful replicate method.

Checking the other candidates once more — the sun's straight-edged glitter path reads as broken glints rather than a hard road edge, the sailboat and rose sky band both read correctly at whole view, and the headland ledge is fine as accepted — I'm confident the painting is in a genuinely resolved state. Nothing this sitting changed on the actual painting itself; the scratch trial on the streak confirmed it's a texture fault that can't be fixed by a body cover, which itself informed the decision not to attempt further repairs, and I think the honest, well-reasoned call now is to finish rather than force another unnecessary cover.

I don't think a signature is necessary or worth the risk of a new mark. I want to write up the final journal entries covering each open passage's judgement, the reasoning behind this sitting's decisions, the lessons worth carrying forward, and an updated handoff — but first I'll take one more clean look at the whole painting, just to ground my closing reflection in its actual current state before finishing.
